rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero information about which modality, encoder, profile setting, or aggregation strategy is most effective. The entire design space is unexplored. 2) What this tests: config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) establishes the simplest possible baseline—a single-modality, single-profile model with a standard linear dimensionality reduction. It answers the foundational question: how well does a minimal RNA-only model perform, and what is the floor of the search space? 3) Why it is the best first experiment: With no prior evidence, the most efficient use of the first experiment is to anchor the search with a fast, interpretable, low-complexity baseline. This gives a clear reference point against which all subsequent experiments (other encoders, multiprofile, image-only, multimodal, different aggregations/fusions) can be meaningfully compared. It also trains quickly, reducing the risk that the first experiment is uninformative or fails. Starting here avoids the trap of jumping to a complex multimodal configuration whose performance cannot be attributed to any specific design choice without a simple reference.

We have only one completed experiment (config_001: RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA → 48.5% acc), leaving almost all design dimensions unexplored. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether the image modality carries discriminative signal at all. Config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is the cleanest unimodal baseline for the image side, structurally parallel to config_001 (singleprofile, no aggregation, no fusion). If image-only performs competitively with or above the RNA baseline, it justifies investing subsequent experiments in multimodal fusion and aggregation. If it performs poorly, we can redirect the budget toward RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. This experiment isolates the image modality's standalone contribution without confounding it with fusion strategy or multiprofile complexity, making it the highest-information-gain choice under a tight budget.

Evidence: config_001 (RNA, single profile, PCA n2000) achieves 48.5% accuracy, while config_010 (Image, single profile, ResNet50) achieves only 20.8%, establishing RNA as the dominant signal and leaving large uncertainty about whether multiprofile aggregation can improve the RNA baseline. Question: config_002 directly extends config_001 by switching from single to multiprofile with avgpool aggregation while keeping the same PCA n2000 encoder, cleanly isolating the effect of profile multiplicity and aggregation on RNA performance. Why this is the best next experiment: With only two data points, the highest-value question is whether the multiprofile design axis adds value over the current best single-profile setup. A positive result would justify investing further in multiprofile + aggregation variants (and ultimately multimodal multiprofile configs); a negative or neutral result would redirect effort toward encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt) or multimodal fusion with single profiles. This experiment changes only the profile/aggregation dimension relative to the current best, making it the cleanest and most informative next step under a limited budget.

Evidence: config_002 (multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a large jump over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is the most impactful design choice so far. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.208), so RNA is the dominant signal. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple avgpool for combining multiple profiles—this is the key mechanism enabling the multiprofile gain. This experiment (config_003) isolates exactly one variable (aggregation: transformer vs avgpool) while holding RNA encoder (pca_n2000) and profile setting (multiprofile) constant, giving a clean comparison against config_002. If transformer substantially exceeds avgpool, it tells us the aggregation architecture is a high-leverage knob to exploit in later multimodal experiments; if not, avgpool is sufficient and we can redirect budget toward encoder or fusion choices. Under a tight budget, this single-variable test on the strongest-performing branch is the most information-efficient next step.

Evidence: RNA-only with multi-profile + avgpool (config_002, PCA n2000) is the best result so far (0.591 acc), substantially outperforming single-profile RNA (0.485) and image-only ResNet50 (0.208). Avgpool clearly beats transformer for aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519). However, only PCA n2000 has been tested as an RNA encoder, leaving a major uncertainty: does a learned representation (scVI) improve on the linear PCA baseline in the best-performing multi-profile + avgpool setting? Question: config_005 (RNA-only, multi-profile, scvi_n200, avgpool) isolates the RNA encoder as the single variable changed relative to config_002, directly testing whether a nonlinear learned embedding outperforms PCA. Why this is the best next experiment: Before committing budget to multimodal fusion (which adds image encoder, fusion strategy, and more hyperparameters), we need to know whether the RNA backbone can be improved. If scvi substantially beats PCA here, it reshapes which multimodal configs to prioritize; if it does not, PCA remains the efficient choice and we can focus budget on fusion design. This is a clean, single-variable comparison that maximizes information per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.650 vs config_002 (pca_n2000, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.591, suggesting scvi improves performance by ~0.06. However, this comparison is confounded because both use multiprofile+avgpool. The singleprofile PCA baseline (config_001) is 0.485. Uncertainty: Is the scvi improvement driven by the encoder itself or by an interaction with multiprofile? config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) directly isolates the encoder effect by changing only the RNA encoder relative to config_001. If scvi-singleprofile substantially exceeds 0.485, the encoder matters independently and we should prioritize encoder choice in multimodal designs. If it remains near 0.485, the gain is profile-interaction-driven, shifting focus to aggregation. This single-variable comparison is the most efficient way to reduce uncertainty about a core design axis before committing budget to more complex multimodal configurations.

Evidence: The best configuration so far is config_005 (rna_only, scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) at 0.650 acc, while image_only with resnet50 is very weak (0.208). We have strong evidence that RNA dominates and that scvi_n200 + multiprofile + avgpool is the optimal RNA pipeline. The key remaining uncertainty is whether adding the image modality via fusion provides any complementary signal beyond the already-strong RNA representation. Question tested: config_030 (multimodal, scvi_n200, multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, concat) directly compares against config_005 by adding only the image branch and a simple concat fusion, isolating the marginal contribution of image. Why best next: It uses the already-validated best RNA settings so any performance change is attributable to the image modality and fusion. If it improves, it justifies further investment in multimodal and stronger image encoders; if it does not, it efficiently rules out multimodal as a direction and lets us focus remaining budget on RNA encoder improvements (e.g., scgpt) or aggregation refinements. This is a single-variable change from the current best, making it the most informative use of one experiment.

Evidence: The best rna_only config (config_005: scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) achieves 0.650 acc, while the only multimodal test (config_030: same RNA settings + resnet50, concat fusion) scores 0.632 — slightly worse. Image-only (config_010) is very weak (0.208), suggesting resnet50 features may be noisy or uninformative. The key uncertainty is whether the small multimodal deficit is due to the concat fusion failing to handle modality imbalance, or whether the resnet50 image features are simply unhelpful. This experiment (config_031) changes only the fusion from concat to weighted, holding all other settings identical to config_030. If weighted fusion recovers the gap to ~0.650+, it shows the image carries marginal signal that concat was diluting; if it does not, it strongly indicates the resnet50 image features are not useful and we should pivot to testing a stronger image encoder (ViT-L) or focus further on RNA-only improvements. This single-variable comparison is the most efficient way to isolate the fusion effect before committing further budget to multimodal variants.

The current best configuration is config_031 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, weighted; acc=0.678). The only aggregation tested with scvi_n200 in the multimodal setting is avgpool. For pca_n2000, avgpool clearly outperformed transformer (0.591 vs 0.519), but scvi_n200 produces a learned latent representation that may interact differently with attention-based aggregation. Config_033 changes only the aggregation (avgpool → transformer) relative to the current best, cleanly isolating this design choice. If transformer improves performance, it identifies a new best and a promising direction; if it does not, it confirms avgpool is optimal for scvi and frees subsequent experiments to probe the image encoder (ViT-L) or RNA encoder (scgpt) as the next lever. This is the highest-information single-variable test available under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best is config_033 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) at 0.7131 acc. Within the same family, avgpool+concat (0.6315) → avgpool+weighted (0.6776) shows a ~4.6pp gain from weighted fusion. However, we have not yet tested whether this fusion advantage persists when aggregation is switched to transformer. Question: config_032 (identical to config_033 except fusion=concat) isolates the single variable of fusion method under transformer aggregation. If concat ≈ weighted, then fusion choice is secondary to aggregation and we can simplify the design; if concat << weighted, it confirms weighted fusion is essential regardless of aggregation. Why this is the best next experiment: it is a clean one-variable comparison against the current best, has the highest expected performance among untested configs, and directly reduces uncertainty about whether the weighted-fusion gain seen with avgpool generalizes to transformer—information that determines which fusion strategy to lock in before exploring other axes (e.g., scgpt encoder or ViT-L image backbone).
